newsitem.title: USA: Carolina Power prepares for thrashing from Fran.
newsitem.headline: Carolina Power prepares for thrashing from Fran.

text.p: Carolina Power & Light Co. was enlisting help Thursday from across the South to help it cope with what looks like an inevitable tangle of downed lines and trees as Hurricane Fran takes aim at the Carolinas.
"If the hurricane follows its current track, we are the main utility in its way," said Carolina Power spokeswoman Sally Ramey. "It's a huge storm."

By 1 p.m. EDT, less than 12 hours before Fran's leading edge was set to strike the coast, Carolina Power had mustered 1,200 linemen from utilities and contractors as far away as Alabama, Kentucky, and Virginia to join its own 1,000-strong crew.
"Yesterday, our emergency planners were also talking about bringing in 70 extra tree clearing crews, and they were wondering if that's too few," said Ramey.
Meteorologists are predicting Fran will make landfall somewhere near the North-South Carolina border, with hurricane winds extending 145 miles from the eye of the storm.
"We have been in close contact with the National Weather Service, and are expecting winds perhaps as strong as 125-140 miles per hour (mph) as it hits the coast," she said.
"The damage we are expecting is potentially much more than Bertha in July," Ramey said, referring to the hurricane that quickly brushed along North Carolina's coast in July.

"But Fran is a slow-moving storm, so we may not be able to start assessing damage until late Friday and probably won't know the full extent of it until sometime Saturday because of the high winds and rain," said Ramey.

Bertha, at its peak, left 225,000 of Carolina Power's 1.1 million customers without power. That customer base represents over three million residents in the Carolinas, most of them in central and eastern North Carolina.

Most at risk during the storm is Carolina Power's 5,867 miles of transmission lines, the high-voltage lines carrying power from generating facilities to local distribution networks, and the neighbourhood distribution lines themselves.

Earlier Thursday the company said it had shut down its 1,521 megawatt (MW) Brunswick nuclear power facility in Southport, N.C., a site near North Carolina's southernmost and quite close to Fran's current path.
